title: Assignment: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
I’ve been thinking about how uneven car access is across Philadelphia. In some parts of the city, almost everyone owns a car; in others, most households don’t have one at all. If I am a transit or planning agency deciding where to add bus service, put in bike lanes, or expand car-share, I would want to know which tracts are most dependent on alternatives to driving. So the question I set out to answer is: what kinds of places in Philadelphia have the highest share of households without a vehicle, and what can we predict about that share?
To measure it, I use ACS table B08203, which counts households by how many vehicles they have:

B08203_001: total households
B08203_002: households with no vehicle available

From those two counts I build my outcome, the percent of households with no vehicle in each tract. I picked this over median rent or home value because it’s a clean rate that I can give a proper margin of error, and it’s a number that genuinely matters for policy decisions on the ground.

Part 0: Setup

library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)
library(sf)
library(caret)

Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY") != ""   # should print TRUE


[1] TRUE



The cross-validation helper


Code
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1: don't drop rows).")
  }
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)
  fit$results$RMSE
}




The model log


Code
model_log <- tibble(
  model   = character(),
  added   = character(),
  cv_rmse = numeric(),
  notes   = character()
)

The CV RMSE: On tracts it hasn’t seen, the baseline model misses by about 11.9 percentage points of no-vehicle households. In other words, a transit planner relying on just income, poverty, renter share, and commute time would be off by roughly 12 points for a typical unseen tract — a wide margin, which is why I go looking for spatial context next.


2C: Where is the baseline wrong?


Code
tracts <- tracts %>% mutate(resid_m1 = residuals(m1))

ggplot(tracts) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = resid_m1), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "grey95", high = "#b2182b", midpoint = 0) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Baseline model: where it's wrong",

       fill = "Residual")









Answer: The red clusters (model under-predicting) sit in the lower-income, higher-density parts of North and West Philly, and the blue ones (over-predicting) are mostly in wealthier outlying tracts. What those red places probably have in common is a transportation context the ACS predictors just can’t see — how close they are to rapid transit or bike stations, how safe the streets feel, how walkable they are. That’s exactly why I pull crime, shooting, and Indego station data in Part 3.

text:
Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal


Code
carto_get <- function(sql) {
  url <- paste0("https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=", URLencode(sql))
  st_read(url, quiet = TRUE)
}



Worked example: residential burglaries in 2023


Code
burglary <- carto_get(
  "SELECT the_geom, text_general_code, dispatch_date
   FROM incidents_part1_part2
   WHERE dispatch_date >= '2023-01-01' AND dispatch_date < '2024-01-01'
     AND text_general_code = 'Burglary Residential'"
) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts)) %>%
  filter(!st_is_empty(.))

nrow(burglary)


[1] 3681




Shooting victims (second Carto layer)


Code
shootings <- carto_get(
  "SELECT the_geom, date_
   FROM shootings
   WHERE date_ >= '2021-01-01' AND date_ < '2024-01-01'"
) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts)) %>%
  filter(!st_is_empty(.))

nrow(shootings)


[1] 6280




Indego stations (Week 4 feed, not Carto)


Code
stations <- st_read("https://www.rideindego.com/stations/json/", quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))


Answer: I picked these three layers because they get at the street-level reality my baseline model was missing. Crime and shootings tell me how safe it actually feels to walk or bike to transit — nobody is giving up the car if the block doesn’t feel safe. And the Indego stations tell me whether a real car-free alternative is even there. That’s the kind of thing the ACS variables, for all their detail, just can’t describe.

title: Assignment: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 4: Building spatial features

4A–4B: Counting and density


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    n_burglary = lengths(st_intersects(., burglary)),
    n_shoot    = lengths(st_intersects(., shootings)),
    area_sqmi  = as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 27878400,
    burglary_per_sqmi = n_burglary / area_sqmi,
    shoot_per_sqmi    = n_shoot / area_sqmi
  )




4C: Distance to nearest station


Code
tract_pts <- st_point_on_surface(tracts)
nearest_idx <- st_nearest_feature(tract_pts, stations)

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_station_mi = as.numeric(
    st_distance(tract_pts, stations[nearest_idx, ], by_element = TRUE)) / 5280)




4D: Distance to City Hall


Code
city_hall <- st_sfc(st_point(c(-75.1636, 39.9526)), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_ch_mi = as.numeric(st_distance(tract_pts, city_hall)) / 5280)




4E: Fit, cross-validate, log after each feature


Code
# m2: crime density
f2 <- y ~ med_incE + poverty_rate + rent_pct + commute_min + burglary_per_sqmi + shoot_per_sqmi

model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m2", added = "crime + shooting density",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f2, tracts),
          notes = "density features")

# m3: distance to nearest bike station
f3 <- y ~ med_incE + poverty_rate + rent_pct + commute_min + dist_station_mi

model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m3", added = "distance to nearest Indego station",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f3, tracts),
          notes = "nearest-distance feature")

# m4: distance to City Hall
f4 <- y ~ med_incE + poverty_rate + rent_pct + commute_min + dist_ch_mi

model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m4", added = "distance to City Hall",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f4, tracts),
          notes = "single-place distance")

model_log


# A tibble: 4 × 4
  model added                              cv_rmse notes                        
  <chr> <chr>                                <dbl> <chr>                        
1 m1    ACS baseline (4 predictors)           11.9 linear, no spatial features …
2 m2    crime + shooting density              11.4 density features             
3 m3    distance to nearest Indego station    10.9 nearest-distance feature     
4 m4    distance to City Hall                 10.1 single-place distance        


Answer: I built five spatial features and logged three models. The one that helped most was distance to City Hall (m4), which cut CV RMSE from 11.9 to 10.1. Distance to the nearest Indego station (m3) also helped, down to 10.9 — I was sure it would, since it directly measures car-free access, and it did. The surprise was crime and shooting density (m2): it only nudged things to 11.4, basically nothing. I think that’s because crime density tracks income and density so closely that the ACS baseline had already captured most of what it had to offer.

Answer: The transformation that helped most was the squared distance to City Hall (m6), which brought CV RMSE down to 9.59 — the best of the whole log — because the relationship between distance and car-lessness clearly bends and flattens rather than running straight. The log of crime density (m5, 11.2) barely beat the raw-density model, and the distance rings (m7, 10.2) sat in between. For my categorical variable, ringOuter is the coefficient for outer tracts against the reference level Core: it tells me how much higher or lower the predicted no-vehicle share is in an outer tract compared to a core one, holding everything else fixed.

title: Assignment: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 7: Reflection
1. What helped, and what didn’t? The single most useful move was squaring the distance to City Hall (m6), which took CV RMSE from 10.1 down to 9.59 — distance and car-lessness don’t run in a straight line, and letting the model bend that relationship bought the most. The biggest disappointment was crime and shooting density (m2): I was sure street safety would matter, but it only moved CV RMSE from 11.9 to 11.4. Crime density is so tightly tied to income and density that the ACS baseline had already absorbed almost everything it could offer. The other notable thing is that my “final” model (10.7) didn’t actually beat the simpler squared-distance model (9.59) — piling on every helpful feature cost more than it gained, a useful reminder that more is not always better in CV RMSE terms.
2. Read one coefficient twice. Take I(dist_ch_mi^2). In its β̂ reading, the estimated coefficient is about -0.15, meaning the squared distance term pulls the curve downward as distance grows. In its ŷ reading, because the linear distance term is positive and this squared term is negative, predicted no-vehicle share rises with distance from Center City at first and then flattens or turns down — exactly the bend I saw in the scatterplot.
3. What’s still missing? On the final residual map, the places I still miss most are the very high-density core and a few outlying tracts with almost nobody in them. The next thing I’d want to measure is transit service intensity — how many bus routes run through a tract, or how frequent the service is — because whether a household gives up the car depends as much on how good the transit is as on whether transit exists. SEPTA’s route data, or a transit layer on OpenDataPhilly, is where I’d go for that.
4. How much of the remaining error might be noise? The last plot tells the story: the biggest misses sit in tracts where the outcome estimate itself has a high CV. That points to a good chunk of the leftover error being sampling uncertainty in the ACS number rather than a missing predictor — if the estimate itself is only known to within a wide band, there’s no model that can predict it more tightly than that.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.

section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

  mutate(moe_pct =moe /estimate* 100)

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
When using data from the ACS to analyze urban policy, we need to pay attention to the margin of error, particularly for small, sparsely populated counties. In California, counties with extremely small populations, such as Sierra County, have very high relative errors, so we cannot rely too heavily on rent estimates from these counties when making policy decisions.
The primary source of this uncertainty is the small sample size of the survey. Because the number of survey respondents is limited, the estimates are subject to greater variation.
Before applying census spatial data in urban planning work, we should check if these estimates are reliable. We cannot take every ACS figure as a hard truth. Recognizing estimation errors prevents us from making poor policy decisions that rely on shaky statistical results.

title: Verify the Claim: Poverty Rate Change in Philadelphia Census Tracts
text:
Part 1: Reconstruct
The WHYY story compares poverty across Philadelphia neighborhoods using two separate 5-year ACS datasets: 2006–2010 and 2013–2017. I pull data from ACS table B17001, which tracks population counts grouped by poverty status:

B17001_001: Total population counted for poverty calculations
B17001_002: People with incomes below the poverty threshold

I use the acs5 product here because the news article relies on these 5-year rolling ACS estimates.

Assumptions
This analysis runs at the census tract level, not the custom neighborhood boundaries the reporter used. The journalist combined several census tracts to create their own neighborhood areas and did not share which tracts went into each neighborhood. That means my tract-level results will not perfectly match the neighborhood numbers shown in the article.
I am assuming the article uses the standard ACS poverty definition found in table B17001.
Some tracts return NA values, mostly areas with no permanent residents, such as airports or large industrial sites. I will drop these tracts from my analysis.


Overlap Check
These two ACS time windows, 2006–2010 and 2013–2017, do not overlap. There is a two-year gap between them. The survey samples are independent, so I can calculate changes over time without worrying about bias caused by overlapping samples.


Show code
phl_0610 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  year = 2010,
  survey = "acs5",
  variables = c(total = "B17001_001", poverty = "B17001_002")
) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = c(estimate, moe)) %>%
  rename(
    total_0610 = estimate_total,
    moe_total_0610 = moe_total,
    poverty_0610 = estimate_poverty,
    moe_poverty_0610 = moe_poverty
  )

phl_1317 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  year = 2017,
  survey = "acs5",
  variables = c(total = "B17001_001", poverty = "B17001_002")
) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = c(estimate, moe)) %>%
  rename(
    total_1317 = estimate_total,
    moe_total_1317 = moe_total,
    poverty_1317 = estimate_poverty,
    moe_poverty_1317 = moe_poverty
  )

phl_tract <- inner_join(phl_0610, phl_1317, by = c("GEOID", "NAME"))

title: Verify the Claim: Poverty Rate Change in Philadelphia Census Tracts
text:
Part 2: Test
I calculate poverty rates and their associated margins of error using the moe_prop() function. Jurjevich and co-authors (2018) set reliability rules based on coefficient of variation (CV):

CV < 12%: Reliable
12% ≤ CV ≤ 40%: Somewhat reliable
CV > 40%: Unreliable

I compute the poverty rate change between the two time periods, plus the MOE for this change. I test statistical significance at the 90% confidence level. A change counts as statistically distinguishable from zero when the absolute value of the z-score is greater than 1.645.


Show code
phl_tract_calc <- phl_tract %>%
  mutate(
    povrate_0610 = poverty_0610 / total_0610,
    moe_povrate_0610 = moe_prop(poverty_0610, total_0610, moe_poverty_0610, moe_total_0610),
    cv_0610 = (moe_povrate_0610 / 1.645) / povrate_0610 * 100,
    reliability_0610 = case_when(
      cv_0610 < 12 ~ "Reliable",
      cv_0610 <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE ~ "Unreliable"
    ),
    povrate_1317 = poverty_1317 / total_1317,
    moe_povrate_1317 = moe_prop(poverty_1317, total_1317, moe_poverty_1317, moe_total_1317),
    cv_1317 = (moe_povrate_1317 / 1.645) / povrate_1317 * 100,
    reliability_1317 = case_when(
      cv_1317 < 12 ~ "Reliable",
      cv_1317 <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE ~ "Unreliable"
    ),
    povrate_change = povrate_1317 - povrate_0610,
    se_1 = moe_povrate_0610 / 1.645,
    se_2 = moe_povrate_1317 / 1.645,
    se_diff = sqrt(se_1^2 + se_2^2),
    moe_change = se_diff * 1.645,
    z_score = povrate_change / se_diff,
    sig_change = abs(z_score) > 1.645
  ) %>%
  drop_na(povrate_change)

summary_sig <- phl_tract_calc %>%
  summarise(
    total_tracts = n(),
    tracts_sig_change = sum(sig_change, na.rm = TRUE),
    tracts_no_sig_change = sum(!sig_change, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

title: Verify the Claim: Poverty Rate Change in Philadelphia Census Tracts
text:
Part 3: Adjudicate
The WHYY article argues that poverty grew across many Philadelphia neighborhoods, and that large numbers of white residents are living below the poverty line. I sort these claims into three buckets based on my tract-level analysis.
Supported: Many census tracts show statistically significant increases in poverty rate between 2006–2010 and 2013–2017. The broad direction of the article — rising poverty in parts of Philadelphia — is consistent with the data. The existence of white residents in poverty across the city is also a real population pattern.
Not supported: The article presents neighborhood-level poverty numbers without reporting any margins of error. Some of the apparent increases it highlights are within the ACS sampling error and cannot be distinguished from random noise. Treating these estimates as precise facts overstates what the data actually tells us.
Cannot be determined: The reporter aggregated tracts into custom neighborhood boundaries and never published which tracts belong to which neighborhood. I cannot replicate the exact neighborhood-level figures from the story, so I cannot verify whether the specific neighborhoods named in the article moved in the direction claimed.
Overall, the headline trend is broadly consistent with the data, but the article ignores statistical uncertainty and presents small-area estimates as if they were exact counts.

title: Verify the Claim: Poverty Rate Change in Philadelphia Census Tracts
text:
Part 4: Rewrite
New census estimates show rising poverty across many Philadelphia neighborhoods, with a notable share of white residents living below the poverty line. But not every neighborhood’s poverty shift is statistically meaningful. ACS estimates carry sampling error, and small-area numbers can be noisy. While many tracts show real, measurable increases, some apparent changes may only reflect random survey variation. These findings confirm inequality persists across Philadelphia, but neighborhood poverty figures should be read with caution.

title: Assignment 5: House Price Prediction, Chicago
text:
We predict single-family sale prices in Chicago from 2023 to 2025. Starting with a structure-only model, we add accessibility, neighborhood, property, and time features, then compare transformations using the same ten validation folds.
The selected model reduces mean ten-fold RMSE from $285,974 for the previous model to $250,171, a 12.5% improvement. The outcome remains the original sale price in dollars throughout. The comparison uses ordinary linear regression with the predictor logs, squared terms, categories, and interactions covered in class.

Part 1: Clean and look first

1A: Keep the same training sample
We remove nominal sales, implausibly low prices per square foot, and structures smaller than 300 square feet. These rules are applied once. We keep luxury sales and multi-property transactions in every validation comparison; removing their large errors would make a different prediction task look artificially easier. Every test house is retained.

keep_2 <- keep_1 & train_raw$sale_price / (train_raw$building_000sf * 1000) >= 20

cleaning_log <- tibble(
  Rule = c("Sale price at least $10,000", "Price per square foot at least $20",
           "Building at least 300 square feet"),
  Removed = c(sum(!keep_1), sum(keep_1 & !keep_2), sum(keep_2 & !keep_3))
) %>% mutate(Remaining = nrow(train_raw) - cumsum(Removed))
stopifnot(identical(as.numeric(d$id), as.numeric(train_raw$id[keep_3])))

1B: Sale prices, size, time, and location


Show code
p_price <- ggplot(d, aes(sale_price)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 45, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())) +

  geom_point(alpha = 0.12, size = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "steelblue") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())) +
  labs(title = "Size alone leaves large differences", x = "Building size (000 sq ft)",
       y = "Sale price")
p_year <- d %>% group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(median_price = median(sale_price), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(factor(year), median_price, group = 1)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue") + geom_point() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_dollar()) +
  labs(title = "Median sale price by year", x = "Year", y = "Median price")
p_location <- ggplot(train_sf) +
  geom_sf(aes(color = sale_price), size = 0.3, alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(trans = "log10",
                       labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())) +
  theme_void() + labs(title = "Prices vary across Chicago", color = "Price")
(p_price + p_size) / (p_year + p_location)









Sale prices are strongly right-skewed, and similarly sized houses can sell for very different amounts. Location and the upper tail therefore matter alongside structure. Year and quarter are treated as categories so the model can represent market and seasonal differences without imposing a straight-line quarterly trend.

title: Assignment 5: House Price Prediction, Chicago
text:
Part 2: Build and compare models

2A: Keep the outcome in dollars
The Week 7 rule is “Log X, keep Y in dollars.” Every candidate below uses sale_price as its response. We use lm() with predictor logs, squared terms written with I(), factors, and interactions; the model log also tests the pooled neighborhood fixed effects discussed in the lecture.
All candidates use the same 23,099 training sales and the same ten folds as the previous model. We reproduce its CV RMSE of $285,973.56 before comparing changes. Missing property values are filled using each training fold only. RMSE is the average of the ten fold-level RMSEs; MAE, R², and Moran’s I use all out-of-fold predictions.


Show code
xy <- st_coordinates(train_sf)
w <- nb2listw(knn2nb(knearneigh(xy, k = 5)), style = "W")
base_rhs<-paste('building_000sf + building_age + num_bedrooms + num_full_baths +',
 'dist_downtown_mi + dist_cta_mi + mean_3cta_mi + cta_within_half_mile +',
 'log(med_income) + pct_poverty + pct_bachelors + pct_owner_occ + pct_vacant +',
 'log(med_rent) + building_000sf:log(med_income)')
f12<-as.formula(paste('sale_price ~',base_rhs))
set.seed(5080)
reference_fit<-train(f12,data=d,method='lm',trControl=trainControl(method='cv',number=10))
folds<-reference_fit$control$index
stopifnot(abs(reference_fit$results$RMSE-285973.56)<1)

# All candidate responses are the original dollar price.
candidates<-list()
add<-function(id,description,rhs) {
 candidates[[id]]<<-list(id=id,description=description,rhs=rhs)
}
physical<-paste('lotsize_acre + num_half_baths + num_fireplaces + garage_size +',
 'central_air + one_story + full_basement + finished_basement + brick_stone_ext + warmairfurnace')
time_terms<-'factor(year) + factor(sale_qrt) + is_multisale'
rich<-paste(base_rhs,physical,time_terms,sep=' + ')
landlog<-gsub('lotsize_acre','log(lotsize_acre)',rich,fixed=TRUE)
counts<-landlog
caps<-c(num_bedrooms=6,num_full_baths=5,num_half_baths=2,num_fireplaces=3,garage_size=3,cta_within_half_mile=3)
for(v in names(caps))counts<-gsub(v,paste0('factor(pmin(',v,',',caps[[v]],'))'),counts,fixed=TRUE)
geo_terms<-'lon_c + lat_c + I(lon_c^2) + I(lat_c^2) + lon_c:lat_c'
curves<-'I(building_000sf^2) + I(building_age^2)'
raw_context<-gsub('log(med_income)','med_income',landlog,fixed=TRUE)
raw_context<-gsub('log(med_rent)','med_rent',raw_context,fixed=TRUE)
add('m12_reference','Previous model: log income/rent + size-income interaction',base_rhs)
add('raw_income','Previous model with raw income',gsub('log(med_income)','med_income',base_rhs,fixed=TRUE))
add('raw_context','Previous model with raw income/rent',gsub('log(med_rent)','med_rent',gsub('log(med_income)','med_income',base_rhs,fixed=TRUE),fixed=TRUE))
add('log_size','Previous model with logged building size',gsub('building_000sf','log(building_000sf)',base_rhs,fixed=TRUE))
add('extra_attributes','Add physical attributes, time and multi-sale',rich)
add('log_lot','Additional attributes; log lot size',landlog)
add('log_lot_squared','Log lot size + its square',paste(landlog,'I(log(lotsize_acre)^2)',sep=' + '))
add('size_squared','Log lot size + building size squared',paste(landlog,'I(building_000sf^2)',sep=' + '))
add('age_squared','Log lot size + building age squared',paste(landlog,'I(building_age^2)',sep=' + '))

for(v in c('dist_cta_mi','mean_3cta_mi','dist_downtown_mi'))distance_log<-gsub(v,paste0('log1p(',v,')'),distance_log,fixed=TRUE)
add('log_distances','Log lot size + logged distance predictors',distance_log)
add('coordinates_linear','Log lot size + linear coordinates',paste(landlog,'lon_c + lat_c',sep=' + '))
add('coordinates_squared','Log lot size + coordinate squares and interaction',paste(landlog,geo_terms,sep=' + '))
add('coordinates_categories','Coordinate squares + grouped counts',paste(counts,geo_terms,sep=' + '))
add('coordinates_full','Coordinate squares + grouped counts + size/age squares',paste(counts,geo_terms,curves,sep=' + '))

add('facility_interactions','Coordinate model + size by air-conditioning/single-story',paste(counts,curves,geo_terms,'building_000sf:central_air + building_000sf:one_story',sep=' + '))




2B: Try changes that have a reason
We first add the existing property, land, and sale-time attributes. We then compare raw versus logged predictors, squares of size and age, and grouped count variables. For location, we test linear coordinates, their squares, and their interaction; area-by-coordinate interactions allow an extra square foot to have different dollar value in different places. Centering longitude at −87.65 and latitude at 41.88 makes the coordinate terms easier to calculate and leaves their model information unchanged.
The alternative tract fixed-effect models use Census tracts as neighborhood categories. Within each training fold, tracts with fewer than 70 sales and unseen validation tracts are pooled into “Other,” following the lecture’s advice to merge sparse categories. No neighboring sale prices, residual lags, or other target-derived predictors are used.


Show code
prepare_fold<-function(tr,va) {
 vars<-c('lotsize_acre','num_half_baths','num_fireplaces','garage_size','warmairfurnace','full_basement')
 for(v in vars){med<-median(tr[[v]],na.rm=TRUE);tr[[v]][is.na(tr[[v]])]<-med;va[[v]][is.na(va[[v]])]<-med}
 # Keep sparse or unseen tract groups pooled; the group rule uses training X only.
 freq<-table(tr$GEOID);common<-names(freq)[freq>=70]
 tr$tract_group<-ifelse(!is.na(tr$GEOID)&tr$GEOID %in% common,tr$GEOID,'Other')
 va$tract_group<-ifelse(!is.na(va$GEOID)&va$GEOID %in% common,va$GEOID,'Other')
 add_variables <- function(x) {
  x$lon_c <- x$lon + 87.65
  x$lat_c <- x$lat - 41.88
  x$age_band <- cut(x$building_age,
    breaks = c(-Inf, 5, 20, 50, 80, 110, Inf), right = TRUE,
    labels = c('0-5', '6-20', '21-50', '51-80', '81-110', '111+'))
  x
 }
 tr <- add_variables(tr)
 va <- add_variables(va)
 list(tr=tr,va=va)
}
fit_predict<-function(cand,tr,va) {
 z<-prepare_fold(tr,va)
 f<-as.formula(paste('sale_price ~',cand$rhs))
 fit<-lm(f,data=z$tr)
 pred<-as.numeric(predict(fit,newdata=z$va))
 stopifnot(length(pred)==nrow(va),all(is.finite(pred)))
 list(pred=pred,fit=fit)
}
score<-function(cand,folds,seed=5080) {
 pred<-rep(NA_real_,nrow(d));fr<-numeric(length(folds))
 for(k in seq_along(folds)) {
  ti<-folds[[k]];vi<-setdiff(seq_len(nrow(d)),ti)
  pred[vi]<-fit_predict(cand,d[ti,],d[vi,])$pred
  fr[k]<-sqrt(mean((d$sale_price[vi]-pred[vi])^2))
 }
 e<-d$sale_price-pred
 metrics<-data.frame(model=cand$id,description=cand$description,seed=seed,
  cv_rmse=mean(fr),pooled_rmse=sqrt(mean(e^2)),mae=mean(abs(e)),median_ae=median(abs(e)),
  oof_r2=1-sum(e^2)/sum((d$sale_price-mean(d$sale_price))^2),
  moran_i=as.numeric(moran(e,w,n=length(e),S0=Szero(w))$I),negative_oof=sum(pred<0))
 list(metrics=metrics,pred=pred)
}

results <- lapply(candidates, score, folds = folds)
model_log <- bind_rows(lapply(results, `[[`, "metrics")) %>% arrange(cv_rmse)
stopifnot(nrow(model_log) == 24,
  abs(results$m12_reference$metrics$cv_rmse -
      reference_fit$results$RMSE) < 0.01)

  "size_age_squared", "count_categories", "coordinates_full",

model_log %>% filter(model %in% key_models) %>%

text:
Part 6: Reflection


Show code
air_beta <- unname(coef(final_fit$fit)["central_air"])


The central-air coefficient is $9,555. Holding the other modeled features fixed, houses with central air are associated with a sale price that is $9,555 higher. For prediction, otherwise identical input records differing only in central air receive predictions that differ by this same dollar amount. This association does not establish the causal effect of installing air conditioning.
The useful changes: logs compress a predictor’s long tail, squares allow a curved relationship, factors allow category differences, and interactions let a relationship vary by place. We keep the outcome in dollars so the model coefficients, predictions, and RMSE remain in dollar units. Better-looking predictor distributions alone are not enough; each choice is assessed using the same validation procedure.
We would not yet deploy the model for assessments. Expensive or unusual transactions still have large errors, residuals remain spatially clustered, and some forecasts are negative. Validation uses random folds rather than future-year or geographic holdouts, and unsold properties may differ from the observed sales. These limitations should accompany the lower CV RMSE.

Code
library(tidyverse)
library(pROC)



The scenario
The Georgia Department of Community Supervision is considering a risk model to guide parole decisions. Every person released to parole would get a predicted probability of being rearrested within three years. The department has two proposed uses:

Use A: people above a threshold get more restrictive supervision (more check-ins, electronic monitoring, faster revocation).
Use B: people above a threshold get priority for reentry services (housing assistance, job placement, a case manager).

The department has promised that the model will not use race. I’ve been hired to build it and to tell them whether that promise means what they think it means.


Part 1: Load and clean


Code
nij <- read_csv("data/nij_recidivism.csv") %>%
  mutate(
    recid              = as.integer(Recidivism_Within_3years == "Yes"),
    male               = as.integer(Gender == "M"),
    age_group          = factor(Age_at_Release),
    prison_years       = factor(Prison_Years,
                                levels = c("Less than 1 year", "1-2 years",
                                           "Greater than 2 to 3 years",
                                           "More than 3 years")),
    prior_fel_arrests  = parse_number(Prior_Arrest_Episodes_Felony),
    prior_misd_arrests = parse_number(Prior_Arrest_Episodes_Misd),
    puma               = factor(Residence_PUMA),
    offense            = replace_na(Prison_Offense, "Missing"),
    sup_level          = replace_na(Supervision_Level_First, "Missing")
  )

train <- nij %>% filter(Training_Sample == 1)
test  <- nij %>% filter(Training_Sample == 0)


A note on one line of the starter code: Recidivism_Within_3years is stored as the text "Yes"/"No", so as.integer() on it returns NA for every row. Converting with == "Yes" first gets a clean 0/1.
1.1 How many people are in train and in test? What share of each was rearrested within three years?


Code

  set        = c("train", "test"),
  n          = c(nrow(train), nrow(test)),
  rearrested = c(sum(train$recid), sum(test$recid)),

1.2 Look at Gang_Affiliated. How many values are missing, and who are they?

6.2 Would putting puma itself into the model make it more or less race-blind?
Your answer: Less. puma is not a race-neutral variable in this data — its Black share ranges from 14% to 89%, and I just showed that the false positive rate tracks that share (r = 0.41). If puma enters the model, a person’s predicted probability would shift according to the racial composition of their neighborhood even though Race is still absent from the formula. The promise “we don’t use race” would then be cosmetic: the model would be using race indirectly, through geography, and it would also overfit 25 place dummies that carry little signal of their own.


Part 7: The memo
Memo to: Deputy Commissioner, Georgia Department of Community Supervision From: Manching Ho, MUSA 5080 Re: Threshold choice and the meaning of “race-blind”
Threshold for Use A (restrictive supervision): 0.65. Here the false positive is the expensive error — it means more check-ins, monitoring, and faster revocation for someone who would not have reoffended, and that cost is paid in liberty. At 0.65 the model’s sensitivity is 53.7% and its specificity is 74.0%: we accept missing about half of the people who will reoffend in exchange for not over-supervising the three-quarters who won’t. I would not go lower. At 0.50 the model labels 69.9% of everyone “high risk” when only 57.4% actually reoffend, which turns restrictive supervision into the default condition of parole. At 0.75 the opposite failure appears: sensitivity falls to 26.6%, so we would miss three-quarters of the people who reoffend just to keep the flagged group small.
Threshold for Use B (reentry services): 0.35. The errors are reversed here. A false positive wastes a slot on someone who would have been fine; a false negative withholds housing or a job from someone who then returns to prison. At 0.35 sensitivity is 94.1% — we reach almost everyone who will reoffend — at a specificity of 24.4%. Offering services too broadly is a budget problem; offering them too narrowly is a public safety and human problem. At 0.50 nearly seven in ten people would qualify, which is not a service program so much as a mailing list. I would accept the low specificity.
“Doesn’t use race” is not the same as “treats people the same.” Race is not in the formula, yet at the 0.50 cutoff the false positive rate is 58.1% for Black parolees and 48.3% for white parolees — roughly ten points. At 0.65 the gap narrows to 28.8% versus 22.4%, but it does not disappear, and it does not flip. The mechanism is the predictors, not the race column: Black parolees in this data are younger (9.6% in the 18–22 group versus 5.3%) and more often have a violent offense (26.2% versus 14.9%), and age and offense are exactly what move the score. Removing Race from the formula removes the label, not the disparity.
I would not deploy this for Use A unless the department publishes false positive rates by race at the operating threshold, sets a ceiling on the gap, and audits each PUMA group separately — because placing puma in the model would smuggle race back in through geography.
